questions.stem: Which of the following is the largest part of the human brain?
questions.explanation: The CEREBRUM is the largest part of the human brain (~85% of total brain mass); divided into left and right HEMISPHERES by the LONGITUDINAL FISSURE and connected by the CORPUS CALLOSUM. Each hemisphere has 4 LOBES: Frontal (movement, speech-Broca's area, personality), Parietal (touch, spatial awareness), Temporal (hearing, memory, speech-Wernicke's area), Occipital (vision). CEREBELLUM ('little brain' — ~10%): balance, coordination, fine motor. MEDULLA OBLONGATA: autonomic control (breathing, heartbeat, BP) — damage = instant death. Between brain-stem and cerebellum is the PONS. The BRAINSTEM = midbrain + pons + medulla.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain is responsible for maintaining balance, posture, and coordinating voluntary movements?
questions.explanation: The CEREBELLUM (located at the back of the brain, below the occipital lobe) is the 'little brain' — it fine-tunes voluntary movements, maintains BALANCE & POSTURE, coordinates gait, and learns motor skills (e.g., riding a bicycle). Damage to cerebellum = ATAXIA (unsteady gait, tremor, inability to perform rapid alternating movements). Frontal lobe = planning, movement (motor cortex), speech. Medulla = involuntary autonomic (breathing, heartbeat). Pituitary = endocrine 'master gland' (not coordination). Parkinson's affects the SUBSTANTIA NIGRA in the midbrain (dopamine production).

questions.stem: A typical human has how many pairs of spinal nerves?
questions.explanation: Humans have 31 PAIRS OF SPINAL NERVES: 8 CERVICAL (C1-C8), 12 THORACIC (T1-T12), 5 LUMBAR (L1-L5), 5 SACRAL (S1-S5), 1 COCCYGEAL. Each pair emerges through intervertebral foramina. In contrast, humans have 12 PAIRS OF CRANIAL NERVES arising from the brain/brainstem (I=Olfactory, II=Optic, III=Oculomotor, IV=Trochlear, V=Trigeminal, VI=Abducens, VII=Facial, VIII=Vestibulocochlear, IX=Glossopharyngeal, X=Vagus [wanderer, longest], XI=Accessory, XII=Hypoglossal). Mnemonic: 'Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Green Vegetables AH'. Vagus nerve (X) is the longest cranial nerve and a key parasympathetic conductor.

questions.stem: Parkinson's disease is caused by the degeneration of neurons producing which neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: PARKINSON'S DISEASE is caused by the progressive death of DOPAMINERGIC NEURONS in the SUBSTANTIA NIGRA (midbrain) — depleting dopamine, leading to tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia (slow movement), postural instability. Treatment: Levodopa (converted to dopamine in brain). First described by James Parkinson (1817, 'An Essay on the Shaking Palsy'). ALZHEIMER'S: loss of ACETYLCHOLINE neurons (→ memory loss); treatment: donepezil (AChE inhibitor). DEPRESSION: low serotonin (SSRIs increase it). HUNTINGTON'S: autosomal dominant genetic, affects GABAergic neurons in striatum. EPILEPSY: abnormal electrical discharges. MYASTHENIA GRAVIS: autoimmune attack on acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junction.

questions.stem: A 'reflex action' like pulling the hand away from a hot object is controlled by which part of the nervous system?
questions.explanation: A REFLEX ACTION is an involuntary, automatic response mediated by a REFLEX ARC in the spinal cord — NOT the brain. The pathway: RECEPTOR (skin thermal receptor) → AFFERENT (sensory) neuron → DORSAL ROOT of spinal cord → INTERNEURON → EFFERENT (motor) neuron via VENTRAL ROOT → EFFECTOR (muscle contracts, hand withdrawn). The brain gets the information AFTER the action (feels the pain). Speed is crucial for safety — reflex typically completes in <0.1 second. Deep tendon reflexes (knee jerk, patellar) are monosynaptic (no interneuron). Polysynaptic reflexes include withdrawal and crossed-extensor reflexes. via reflex arc.

questions.stem: The HYPOTHALAMUS in the human brain is primarily associated with regulating:

options.option_text: Body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, and hormonal functions

questions.explanation: The HYPOTHALAMUS (deep in the diencephalon, below the thalamus) is the master regulator of HOMEOSTASIS. It controls: (1) BODY TEMPERATURE (thermostat); (2) HUNGER (feeding centre) and SATIETY; (3) THIRST (osmoreceptors); (4) SLEEP-WAKE cycle (suprachiasmatic nucleus = master clock); (5) EMOTIONAL responses; (6) SEXUAL behaviour; (7) ANS (autonomic nervous system) control; (8) HORMONAL SECRETIONS via the pituitary — produces releasing hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine) and direct hormones (oxytocin, ADH stored in posterior pituitary). Long-term memory = HIPPOCAMPUS. Conscious movement = primary motor cortex (frontal lobe). Vision = occipital lobe.

questions.stem: The BROCA's area of the brain is responsible for:
questions.explanation: BROCA's area — in the FRONTAL LOBE (typically left hemisphere; inferior frontal gyrus) — controls SPEECH PRODUCTION. Damage (Broca's aphasia / expressive aphasia) → patient understands language but cannot form fluent speech (can only speak telegraphically). Discovered by French physician Paul Broca 1861. WERNICKE's area — in the TEMPORAL LOBE (posterior superior temporal gyrus, left) — handles LANGUAGE COMPREHENSION. Wernicke's aphasia / receptive aphasia → patient speaks fluently but the words are meaningless gibberish; can't understand others. Both connected by the ARCUATE FASCICULUS (damage → conduction aphasia). 90%+ of right-handers have language in left hemisphere; ~70% of left-handers too. speech formation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the longest cell in the human body?
questions.explanation: NEURONS (nerve cells) are the longest cells in the human body. The longest single neuron — the SCIATIC NERVE axon — can extend from the base of the spine to the big toe, a distance of ~1 metre in an adult. Each neuron has: DENDRITES (receive signals), CELL BODY (soma), AXON (transmits signal), MYELIN SHEATH (Schwann cells in PNS, oligodendrocytes in CNS — enable saltatory conduction, up to 120 m/s), AXON TERMINAL (synapse). Human brain has ~86 BILLION neurons. RBCs (smallest, no nucleus, 7-8 μm). Ovum is the LARGEST cell (~0.1 mm, visible to naked eye). Smallest nucleated human cell: granule cells of cerebellum (~5 μm).
